PART 3 ANCILLARY 4 MATERIALS Section Desiccants

1. Scope - Gives guidance on the use of desiccants in packaging which should govern the choice of desiccant in the field of packaging. 2. Terminology 2.0 For the purpose of this standard, the following 2.1 Barrier - Any material providing deterioration to the packaged article. definitions

Absorption 2.4 Hygroscopic - Capable of absorbing water-vapour from the surrounding atmosphere. will continue until an equilibrium is reached and this is dependent upon the conditions of temperature For many substances, this is a reversible process so that if the and relative humidity of the atmosphere. m~oisture content is in excess of the equilibrium value water-vapour will be given off until equilibrium conditions are established. 3. General 3.1 Dampness not only encourages corrosion but can also cause growth of moulds and bacteria even Various steps can be taken to reduce the adverse effect of moisture on a when water is not present. packed article such as application of temporary protective treatment against corrosion to metallic Such direct protection is not practicable for all' articles, specially surfaces or the proofing of textiles. for certain electrical components of scientific and optical instruments. An ideal method of providinprotection in such instances is by using a completely sealed package. There may still be damp al, inside the container, and the moisture may be given off~by cushioning material used to hold the articles in position. Furthermore, few materials used in making sealed packages are completely resistant to penetration of water-vapour and a certain amount of moisture may reach the articles through the walls of the package. Desiccants are, therefore, essentially used to take-up moisture that may be in package from any of these sources. 3.2 Humidity - Air naturally contains moisture in the form of vapour. The quantjly of moisture present in a unit volume is known as absolute humidity. At any particular temperature, the air can hold only a limited amount of water-vapour; the higher its temperature, the more water-vapour the air can hold. Air containing as much water-vapour as it can hold is said to be saturated. If saturated air is cooled, it will give up by condensation just enough of its moisture as liquid water to leave it saturated at the lower temperature. The maximum quantity of moisture which can be held in vapour form by the atmospheric The hygrometric tables and charts provide this data for a whole determined by the temperature. of temperature. air is range

3.2.1 Relative humiditv - Normally air is not saturated .with water-vapour unless it is in close contact with liquid water. The actual amount of mater-vapour present in air (`that is, the absolute humidity) expressed as a percentage of amount the air contains when ~saturated at the same temperature is called the relative humidity or RH. For example, suppose a cubic metre of air contains 5 g of water-vapour and that air if saturated at the same temperature would contain 20 g of watervapour per cubic metre, then the air has a relative humidity of: 5 -20x 100 = 25 percent

Saturated air, of course, has a relative humidity of 100 percent. Q March 1989, BIS I

3.2.2 The relative humidity of atmosphere is the dominating factor in determining whether the It is known, for example, that at corrosion of metals, mould growth. rotting, etc, will take place. ordinary temperatures, corrosion of iron is extremely slow at relative humidities below 60 percent but Mould growth does not. in general, take -place, or is extremely becomes rapid at&higher humidities. Generally, for engineering products a 50 slow unless the relative humidity is above 70 percent. percent relative humidity level has been found to be the critical level and provides a tolerance against a sudden fall in temperature but for other products, other critical levels may apply. 4. Desiccated 4.1 Genera/ the article itself desirable and it relative humidity generally taken Packages The deterior.ation of many articles can be minimized by applying suitable treatment to Sometimes such treatment is not practicable or either during or after manufacture. is still necessary to protect the contents. One method of doing this is to ensure that the of the atmosphere in contact with the item never exceeds a safe limit which is in practice to be 50 percent.

A package that contains a sufficient quantity of suitable desiccant to ensure that the RH within it will not exceed this figure when stored in any part of the world for a specified period is called desiccated package. An essential requirement of such a pack is that it should contain sufficient quantity of a suitable desiccant to reduce the relative humidity wrthin the pack to 50 percent or less and maintain this for the desired period. To assist in maintaining this reduced level of humidrty, the Hermetically sealed metal There are various ways of achieving this. entry of water-vapour is retarded. containers may be used, or the container may incorporate or be made from a water-vapour barrier, that It is rarely possible to exclude air is a material with a high resistarce to the passage of water-vapour. from such packages or to avoid the use of interior packaging materials that contain some moisture. 4.2 Sources of Moisture described below. 4.2.1 For any package, four sources of moisture generally encountered are

The air inside the barrier contains

some water-vapour.

4.2.2 The air outside the barrier is the most important source of moisture even in a sealed container The except a perfectly sealed metal or glass container which may be completely water-vapour proof. way in which the water passes through the sealed barrier is not important here but `waterproof' material Air-tightness is an even less reliable criterion is not necessarily even moderately water-vapour-proof. than waterproofness. The implication of this is that if the relative humidity outside the package is Often in many countries, higher that inside, there is a tendency for moisture to pass into the package. the relative humidity is 80 to 100 percent and since that of the atmosphere inside the package is to be kept below 50 percent, the transmission of water-vapour may be considerable. For example, 4.2.3 Hygroscopic maie:ialsinside the barrier are a considerable source of moisture. wood and paperboard are both hygroscopic and will give up moisture if temperature rises. The packaged item itself may create a problem if it is made`in part from hygroscopic materials. 4.2.4 Trapped water - There is always a possibility of water being trapped within the article, for Certain example, in pumps after testing, or water being entrained in any oil remaining in an oil bath. non-hygroscopic materials used for packaging contain water as a result of their manufacturing process. Expert guidance should be sought to deal with this problem. 5. Factors Governing Choice of Desiccant

5.1 General Management of the Desiccant - A desiccant maintains a safe relative humidity within the package by absorbing most of the moisture from the air and any moisture arising from the goods cr internal hygroscopic materials. It will further absorb any moisture which enters the package through the barrier but only for a calculated period. The desiccant should be in a dustpro-of container that will prevent its spreading throughout the pack and at the same time allow the desiccant to absorb the moisture from the atmosphere within the pack. There are many dehydrating agents that can be used but certain properties such as moistureabsorbing capacity. chemical inertness, etc. make some materials more suitable than others for use as desiccants in packaging. 5.2 important Factors - In the selection considered are given below: of desiccant for a particular pack, the important factors to be

a)

Moisture absorbing capacity of desiccant in relation to bulk and mass - In order to maintain a safe relative humidity inside a desiccated package, it is essential to have present sufficient desiccant to cater for all possible sources of moisture. In order to minimize the space required in the package for desiccant, it is desirable to use materials of high moisture absorbing capacity. 2

IS:l0106(Part3/Sec4)-1988
Stability and physical form of the desiccant - The physical form of the desiccant should by such as to expose maximum surface of desiccant and allow diffusion of package atmosphere through its mass. The desiccant container should be designed to minimize hindrance to such diffusion. These conditions are best satisfied if the desiccant is available in the form of coarse granules, or tablets. The desiccant should retain its form throughout the performance of its `function, should remain solid and dry to the touch and suffer little or no disintegration.
The material

that is, it

should be such that the absorption of moisture is not acleampanied by chemical changes that will cause it to corrode or otherwise damage its container or the article packed. It should not produce a liquid or gas or a significant rise in temperature.

cl

Influence of normal temperature range on the moisture absorbing capacity of desiccant Desiccants remove moisture from the atmosphere in one of the two ways, for example: i) physically, and ii) chemically. Moisture taken up by chemical combination is firmly held and is not liberated increase normally encountered in the environment. by temperature

Moisture taken up physically is held less firmly and an increase in temperature can cause the desiccant to give up moisture to the atmosphere. It is important, therefore, that those desiccants which take up moisture physically should not give it up again in sufficient quantities to affect materially the relative humidity if the temperature rises.

d)

Means of containing the desiccant - It is essential that the moisture in the package should be able to reach the desiccant and that the desiccant or dust from it should not be allowed to spread throughout the package. For this reason, importance is attached to the containers in which the unit quantities of desiccant are held. The considerations discussed in 7 should, therefore, be taken into account in selecting a unit container for the desiccant. The unit containers should be firmly anchored and properly distributed inside the package.
The desiccants may be indicative or non-indicative

e)

type. of moisture ( on losing its activation ) changes in colour.

The indicative

type on absorption

5.3 Summary - The various factors described under 5.2 restrict the number of desiccants that The desiccants most commonly used for packaging are: suitable for packaging. a) Silica gel, b) Activated alumina, and c) Activated clays.

are

5.3.1 For extremely critical packaging conditions where very low relative humidities (below 10 percent) are to be maintained, molecular sieve desiccants should be used. Any of these materials may be suitable in general but for specific application, a final choice should be made only in relation to nature of the article to be packed. Expert guidance should be sought before finally selecting a desiccant for a particular commodity. The following Indian Standards should also be consulted in this regard: IS : 3401-I 979 Silica gel ( second revision ), and IS : 9700-1981 Activated alumina.

The formulae given under 6.2.1 .I for determining the quantity of basic desiccant used in a package cannot be applied to molecular sieve desiccants. Advice should be sought from suppliers of molecular sieve desiccants as to the appropriate conditions and mode of use in each case, 6. Quantity of Desiccant

6.1 The actual quantity of desiccant necessary in any package depends on the following factors. 6.1.1 Type of water-vapour barrier - The layer or layers of the package that are intended to exclude water-vapour constitute the water-vapour barrier. Some barriers will allow the passage of water-vapour only at an extremely slow rate but even at this rate, the relative humidity may become dangerously high in the absence of a desiccant after a few days under humid conditions. 3

IS:10106(Part3/Sec4)-1988
The important factor is the water-vapour transmission rate ( WVTR ) of the barrier material. This rate is determined experimentally under standard conditions and is expressed in grams per square metre per 24 hours. Method for determinating water transmission rate of flexible materials is given in IS : 1060 ( Part 2 )-I 960 `Methods of sampling and test for paper and allied products: Part 2'. Typical figures for WVTR for some of the materials are given in Table 1.

From the transmission rate, it is possible to calculate the quantity of desiccant necessary to keep the relative humidity inside a package below the critical level for any specified pericd under the climatic conditions it is expected to ~encounter. The better the barrier, the less the desiccant required; if no
moisture can enter, no desiccant is required to deal with it though it would still be necessafy moisture derived from interior packaging material and enclosed air. Any seals employed least be as adequate as the barrier material.
Note In service packaging, water-vapour barriers are classified as follows:

to absorb should at

a) Water-vapour resistant - Offering a high resistance to the passage of water-vapour; transmission rate ( WVTR ) shall not exceed 8 g/m2. 24 h when measured at a temperature of 38�C and a relative humidity of 90 percent. b) Water-vapour proof - Offering a high resistance to the passage of water-vapour; the water-vapour transmission rate ( WVTR ) shall not exceed 1 g/m*. 24 h when measured at a temperature of 38�C and a relative humidity of 90 per cent.

6.1.2

Area of the barrier -

The surface area should be kept as small as possible.

6.1.3. Weight of hygroscopic material inside the barrier - Sufficient desiccant should be used to absorb moisture given off by hygroscopic materials such as wood and paperboard present inside the water-vapour barrier and thus reduce the relative humidity to a safe value. All hygroscopic materials tend to reach equilibrium with the surrounding atmosphere at a relatively slow rate. If a desiccant is used, equilibrium is reached between the moisture in the package atmosphere and that in the hygroscopic material and the desiccant. It is necessary, therefore, to include enough desiccant to absorb the moisture that may be given off by the hygroscopic ~mdterial at elevated temperatures and to ensure that the relative humidity can in no circumstances be above 50 percent. 6.1.4 Required period of storage packer and its first opening. 6.2 Calculation of Quantity of Desiccant Required

Part3/Sec4)-1988

6.2.1 Basic desiccant - A series of formulae have been determined which permit the user to calculate the quantity of desiccant required to provide protection under varying modes of usage. ln using these formulae, protection is defined as the maintenance of relative humidity within the package at 50 percent (or less) during the calculated period of storage.

There are several different types of desiccants ( see 5.3 ) which may be used for such applications, As it is not practical to redefine the all of which have a differing moisture absorption capability. formulae for each type of desiccant, the calculations are based on the concept of basic desiccant, the derivation of which is as follows: weight Basic desiccant is defined as a product capable of absorbing at 50 percent relative humidity and 25�C. 27 percent of moisture on its dry

Note - Silica gel manufactured to IS : 3401-I 979 `Silica gel ( second revision)' conforms with this requirement and, therefore, can be equated directly to the basic desiccant quantity calculated in the formulae. if alternative For example desiccant systems are used, it is essential to ascertain the absorption capacity under defined conditions. desiccant, activated clay may absorb 2.0 percent of moisture on its dry weight and where activated clay is not supplied in basic desiccant units then more material in the ratio 27 : 20 or 1'35 times the quantity will. be required to achieve the same absorbancy. Hence using the formulae to calculate basic desiccant requirements for activated clay requires the answer to be multiplied by 1'35 to give the basic desiccant quantity in grams of activated clay.

is in a fully activated

b) it can be reached by the air within over the items in the package; c) it is in perfect condition the barrier; and

as regards its moisture-absorbing

capacity

7.2 Methods of Meeting Desired Conditions meeting these requirements.

7.2.1 The desiccant should be in unit containers such as bags or sachets which securely within the water-vapour barrier so that they will not wander or chafe.

should be fastened

7.2.2 Bags of desiccant are available in vaious sizes providing quantities of any particular desiccant equivalent in moisture-absorbing capacity to weight units of basic desiccant. Commercial desiccants can be obtained in unit containers equivalent to 25 g, 5G g, 100 g, 250 g, 500 g, 1 kg, 2.5 kg, and 5 kg of basic dessicant ( B. D. ). 7.2.3 In order to achieve the requirement mentioned in 7.1 (b ) above, the units should be packed, The latter should be kept closed until the packer is transported and stored in sealed metal containers. ready to transfer and seal the required amount of desiccant into a space within the water-vapour barrier, It is not usually a good policy to obtain the metal container being closed immediately after transfer. a bulk container of such a size that it has to be continually opened and shut in order to withdraw small numbers of units. It is preferable to have a larger number of small bulk containers. Indicator papers enclosed in the container should be checked as a guide whether the desiccant is still in good condition. 7.2.4 The quantity of desiccant required for a particular package can be pre-determined by calculation (see 6.2). The distribution of the desiccant requires careful thought so that, wherever possible, the Where dimensions are critical, the size of the barrier is not increased to accommodate the desiccant. It is often possible to utilize the use of an alternative or thicker barrier material should~be considered. empty spaces within the barrier by breaking down the total quantity of desiccant required into convenient units. For example,~if a package would have to be increased in size to accommodate say, four bags, the substitution of eight or more smaller bags in the empty spaces might serve the purpose without increasing the size. Provided the physical limits of the item to be packaged allow, the I nit containers should be spread as evenly as possible throughout the package rather than be concentrated in one position. 7.2.5 Desiccant should not be removed from its unit container package. Unit containers only should be used. in order to add small quantities to a

It is sometimes advisable to make separate compartments for the necessary unit containers, both for convenience in packing and unpacking, and ease of securing, but if this method is adopted then If hygroscopic adequate provision must be made to ensure a free circulation of air within the barrier. In the packaging material is used for these compartments, due allowance must-be made (see 6.1.3). of certain items, such as precision instruments, it is essential to prevent desiccant dust from escaping Special containers are available for this purpose. from its container. To safeguard against accidental sifting of desiccant from the unit containers, it is advisable that the packaged item be suitably protected so that the dust cannot filter into small orifices, oil holes, etc. 7.2.6 Desiccant which for accidental or other reasons have been exposed to the never be introduced or re-introduced into the barrier. atmosphere should

The expiry date should always be stamped on it is desirable to allow for unforeseen delays in transit. the package. 6
